newsitem.title: USA: UAW, Ford resume labor talks, anticipate deal.
newsitem.headline: UAW, Ford resume labor talks, anticipate deal.

text.p: Negotiations between Ford Motor Co. and the United Auto Workers resumed Monday following a rest break Sunday night, and Ford Chairman Alex Trotman said he hoped a tentative agreement would be reached later in the day.
The two sides bargained over the weekend in marathon sessions toward concluding a new national labour contract.
"I don't really know when they'll be finished. I hope they'll be finished today, but I don't know that," Trotman told reporters before a speech to the Detroit Economic Club.
"I think we're very close to a settlement," Ford spokesman Jon Harmon said. "Rest was a good thing, and now we're optimistic we're going to have a settlement today."
Trotman said there were a number of issues yet to be resolved but said there was no single item as a sticking point in the talks.
He said the company and the union have discussed several possible contract lengths longer than three years but refused to elaborate.
Ford has previously said that it would like an agreement longer than the traditional three-year UAW contract because it would allow the automaker to stabilise its costs over a longer period.

Worries of a strike were low as production at Ford's U.S. parts and assembly plants resumed on normal schedules, Harmon said. The prior three-year labour contract covering the automaker's 105,000 UAW hourly workers expired at midnight on Saturday.
UAW officials said in the morning that the two sides were close to an agreement, but still at odds over the key issue of the use of outside suppliers, known as outsourcing.

In the pact affecting hourly workers, the union has sought to guarantee minimum employment levels and provisions that restrict the company's ability to shift work to outside suppliers, including establishing the right to strike over such decisions.

Also on the table was the length of time it takes for new workers to reach wage parity with veteran workers. In the previous pact, new hires started at 70 percent of the full, $19-an-hour wage, catching up to veteran workers after three years on the job.

Ford and UAW sources also confirmed Sunday that they reached a tentative agreement covering about 750 salaried workers represented by the union, including designers and product development employees. Details of that agreement were not immediately available.

Trotman added that the company needed to maintain a balance in the contract between meeting the union's needs and improving its own efficiency. "One of our key objectives as manufacturers is to maintain as much flexibility and competitiveness as we possibly can," he said.

Trotman said Ford's bargaining teams were continuing to communicate with their counterparts at General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp. , but he declined to say how a Ford-UAW agreement would affect those competitors.
